messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 44
- Gender: Female
- Ethnicity: South Asian
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Retail Worker
- Trauma Type: Witnessed other trauma
- Pcl5: 68

She is a 44-year-old South Asian woman who works the morning shift at a discount retail store in a strip mall. She has been married for seventeen years and lives with her husband and two teenage children. For the first several sessions, she speaks softly, often looking down at her hands, and pauses frequently as though checking whether her words are safe to say.

The traumatic event happened six months ago, on a Tuesday just after the store opened. She was stocking shelves in the home goods aisle when she heard shouting near the front register. A customer—a middle-aged man she had seen before, someone who always bought the same brand of tea—had collapsed. His face was gray, his breath a wet rattle. She watched from behind a display of kitchen towels as two coworkers tried to help. The man’s eyes were open, unblinking. By the time paramedics arrived, he was already gone. She did not touch him, did not speak to him, did not even know his name. She simply watched.

In the weeks that followed, she could not stop seeing his face. It would appear while she was folding clothes, while she was chopping vegetables, while she was lying in bed beside her sleeping husband. The image came without warning—not as a full memory, but as a flash of gray skin, a sound of shallow breathing, the way his hand had flopped against the tile floor. She began to avoid the home goods aisle. She told her manager she had back pain and could only work register. When a customer asks for help finding something near that aisle, she directs them vaguely and stays behind the counter.

At home, she has become short-tempered. Her son’s loud music makes her jump. Her daughter’s laughter sounds like shouting. She no longer watches the evening news because she is afraid she will see someone dying. She stopped cooking with the pressure cooker because the hiss of steam reminds her of the paramedics’ oxygen mask. Her husband has asked if she is sick. She told him it’s just stress from work. She does not tell him about the nightmares—the ones where she is the one on the floor, unable to move, and no one helps.

At work, she now scans the parking lot before her shift. She checks the faces of everyone who walks in. She has memorized the locations of the security cameras. She tells herself it is just being careful. But she knows it is something else. Her heart races when a customer raises their voice. She feels a cold sweat when someone walks too quickly toward the register. She has started taking her breaks in the back stockroom, where there is no window and no one can see her.

She has not told anyone the full story. When her coworkers talk about what happened, she leaves the room. She feels guilty—not for anything she did, but for being present. She wonders why she did not try to help. She wonders if she could have saved him if she had acted sooner. She replays the morning again and again, searching for a different ending.

She is exhausted. Sleep is fragmented. She wakes at 3:00 a.m. most nights with her heart pounding, unsure why. During the day, she has trouble concentrating. She makes mistakes on the register—shortchanging customers, forgetting to scan items. Her manager has noticed. She is afraid of losing her job.

She comes to therapy because her daughter told her she seems “different.” She does not know if talking will help. She is not sure she wants to talk about it at all. But she is tired of being afraid.
